query: Consider the following context: The recent trend of high-entropy alloys (HEAs) was studied extensively for their promising mechanical properties, but individual constituents' effects have remained unexplored. In that context, which method can be used for the effects of changing the percentage of elements of HfNbTaTiZr-HEA on the mechanical properties, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Varying the relative percentages of the constituent elements in a HfNbTaTiZr high-entropy alloy by adjusting the feedstock composition for mechanical alloying followed by spark plasma sintering (SPS) will systematically change its mechanical properties. Specifically, increasing the fraction of larger-atomic-radius elements (such as Hf or Ta) will increase lattice distortion, leading to higher hardness and possibly lower ductility.
generation.material_initial_state: Mechanically alloyed elemental powder mixtures of Hf, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr in an equiatomic or near-equiatomic ratio.
generation.intervention: Systematic variation of one or more constituent elements’ percentages away from the equiatomic composition during powder blending, followed by consolidation using spark plasma sintering under controlled conditions.
generation.conditions: Consistent SPS processing parameters (temperature, pressure, and atmosphere with low oxygen content) for all samples, ensuring that only the compositional variation is the primary variable.
generation.structural_mediator: Degree of lattice distortion and phase stability, as altered by the atomic size mismatch introduced with composition changes.
generation.mechanism: Changing the relative amounts of constituent elements alters the local lattice strain due to differences in atomic sizes, which in turn affects dislocation mobility and the overall balance between hardness and ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples with an increased percentage of larger atoms (e.g., Hf or Ta) will exhibit increased hardness due to greater lattice distortion, while their ductility may decrease relative to the baseline equiatomic composition.
generation.baseline: An equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr HEA processed via SPS under identical conditions.
generation.boundary: Note that measurable effects are expected only when the compositional variations are sufficiently large (e.g., changes in the order of 5–10 at.% or more) to overcome the inherent tolerance of the high-entropy system to compositional fluctuations.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding the exact threshold of compositional change needed to induce significant variations in mechanical properties, and potential interaction effects among elements may complicate the direct correlation between element percentage and properties.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of HfNbTaTiZr-based HEA samples with controlled variations in the percentage of at least one larger element (e.g., Hf or Ta) by ±5 at.% and ±10 at.% from the equiatomic composition. Consolidate all samples using identical SPS parameters. Perform phase analysis (XRD), microstructural characterization (SEM/TEM), hardness measurements (microindentation), and ductility/tensile tests.
measurements: X-ray diffraction for phase determination and lattice parameter shifts
Scanning/transmission electron microscopy for evaluating lattice distortion and microstructure
Tensile tests for ductility and strength measurements
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the systematic compositional variations do not lead to measurable and statistically significant changes in lattice parameters, hardness, or ductility (beyond experimental error), the hypothesis that changing the percentage of constituent elements significantly influences mechanical properties via lattice distortion is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract High entropy alloys (HEA) have been one of the most attractive groups of materials for researchers in the last several years. Since HEAs are potential candidates for many (e.g., refractory, cryogenic, medical) applications, their properties are studied intensively. The most frequent method of HEA synthesis is arc or induction melting. Powder metallurgy is a perspective technique of alloy synthesis and therefore in this work the possibilities of synthesis of HfNbTaTiZr HEA from powders were studied. Blended elemental powders were sintered, hot isostatically pressed, and subsequently swaged using a special technique of swaging where the sample is enveloped by a titanium alloy. This method does not result in a full density alloy due to cracking during swaging. Spark plasma sintering (SPS) of mechanically alloyed powders resulted in a fully dense but brittle specimen. The most promising result was obtained by SPS treatment of gas atomized powder with low oxygen content. The microstructure of HfNbTaTiZr specimen prepared this way can be refined by high pressure torsion deformation resulting in a high hardness of 410 HV10 and very fine microstructure with grain size well below 5
